chapter_summary:
Welcome to the exciting world of web application hacking, a domain where understanding how the internet works is your primary weapon. Before we can ethically hack web applications, we must first grasp their fundamental architecture and the technologies that power them. At its core, a web application is a client-server system. Your web browser acts as the client, sending requests to a web server, which then processes those requests, often interacting with an application server and a database, before sending a response back to your browser. This response is typically HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, which your browser renders into the interactive pages you see every day.

The communication between your browser and the web server primarily happens over HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) or its secure counterpart, HTTPS. HTTP is a stateless protocol, meaning each request from the client to the server is treated as an independent transaction, without any memory of previous requests. This statelessness is often mitigated by mechanisms like cookies and session management, which allow servers to maintain state and track user interactions over time. Understanding HTTP request methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.), headers, and status codes is absolutely crucial for any aspiring web penetration tester. For instance, a `GET` request is typically used to retrieve data, while a `POST` request is used to submit data, often containing user input that can be a source of vulnerabilities. HTTPS adds a layer of encryption using TLS/SSL, protecting the data in transit from eavesdropping and tampering. While HTTPS secures the communication channel, it does not inherently protect against vulnerabilities within the application logic itself.

Web applications are built upon a stack of technologies. On the server side, you'll encounter web servers like Apache HTTP Server, Nginx, or Microsoft IIS, which are responsible for serving static content and routing requests to the appropriate application server. Application servers, such as Apache Tomcat for Java, Gunicorn/uWSGI for Python, or Node.js for JavaScript, execute the dynamic code that generates web pages, handles user input, and interacts with databases. Common database systems include MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, and Oracle. Each layer of this stack introduces potential vulnerabilities, from misconfigurations in the web server to insecure code in the application logic, and exploitable flaws in the database. Client-side technologies, primarily HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, execute directly in the user's browser. While client-side validation can improve user experience, it can never be trusted for security purposes, as an attacker can easily bypass it by manipulating requests before they reach the server. All critical security checks must always be performed on the server side.

Threats to web applications are diverse and constantly evolving, but they generally fall into several key categories. These include injection flaws, where untrusted data is sent to an interpreter as part of a command or query; broken authentication and session management, allowing attackers to compromise user accounts or impersonate legitimate users; cross-site scripting (XSS), enabling attackers to inject malicious client-side scripts into web pages viewed by other users; and insecure direct object references (IDOR), where an attacker can access unauthorized resources by manipulating parameters. Other common threats involve security misconfigurations, sensitive data exposure, and insufficient logging and monitoring. As ethical hackers, our goal is to systematically identify these weaknesses before malicious actors do. We'll be diving deep into each of these specific threats in subsequent chapters, learning both the theory behind them and the practical methods for exploitation and defense. A common mistake beginners make is focusing solely on the "hacking" tools without truly understanding the underlying web technologies. Take the time to understand HTTP, how web servers function, and the basics of how server-side code interacts with databases. This foundational knowledge is paramount. Always remember, when practicing, only target systems for which you have explicit, written permission. Unauthorized access is illegal and unethical.

screens.title: Web Application Concepts and Threats
screens.subtitle: Understand how browsers, servers, and data interact — and where attackers look first

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will build a grounded mental model of modern web applications so you can reason about how attacks work and where to assess risk. We begin by defining a web application as a client–server system: a browser requests pages, a web server routes those requests, an application server runs the logic, and a database stores persistent data. You will learn the practical roles of HTTP and HTTPS, why HTTP is stateless, and how cookies and session management add state back into the system. We will also introduce the most common categories of threats you will encounter — injection, broken authentication, cross-site scripting, insecure direct object references, and configuration problems — and explain why each maps to a different layer of the stack. A concrete example we will use across the lesson is a simple login flow: a browser issues a POST to a login endpoint, the application server verifies credentials, and the database stores the user record. Finally, I’ll warn you of a common beginner mistake: trusting client-side checks. Client-side validation is for convenience, not security. As you go through the chapter, ask how a vulnerability would affect confidentiality, integrity, or availability.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Web apps are layered systems; security failures can come from protocols, servers, application logic, or client behavior — each requires a distinct testing approach.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Overview
Web Application Concepts and Threats
A practical introduction to how browsers, servers, and databases interact — and where vulnerabilities appear.
In this lesson

You will learn architecture, HTTP behavior, threat categories, and a short hands-on inspection activity using browser developer tools.

Why it matters

Finding a vulnerability depends on understanding where data flows and which components enforce security. This knowledge guides effective testing.

Explore Key Topics
Client-Server Flow
Requests, responses, and state mechanisms such as cookies and sessions.
HTTP vs HTTPS
Transport encryption protects data in transit but not application logic.
Threat Categories
Injection, XSS, broken auth, IDOR, misconfigurations and data exposure.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
16:9 HD Classroom
Browser
HTML/CSS/JS
Renders interface, runs client-side code, and issues HTTP requests.
Web Server
Nginx / Apache / IIS
Serves static content and forwards dynamic requests to the app server.
App Server
Node, Tomcat, Gunicorn
Executes server-side code, enforces security logic, and queries databases.
Database
MySQL / PostgreSQL
Stores application data and is a common target for injection attacks.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills to build in this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the architecture of a web application, identify the roles of HTTP and HTTPS, and list the main components such as web servers, application servers, and databases. You will also be able to distinguish client-side from server-side processing and explain why security checks must happen on the server. Next, you will recognize common threat categories that target web applications, like injection and cross-site scripting, and explain where those threats map in the stack. Finally, you will perform a basic inspection of HTTP traffic using browser developer tools to view headers, status codes, and form payloads. Each objective is practical: for example, knowing how to inspect a POST request and its payload allows you to see how user input is transmitted to the server and where sanitation is needed. A common misconception is that HTTPS fixes all security issues — it protects transport but not flawed server logic. These objectives together give you a foundation for both testing and communicating findings to developers.

keyIdea.title: Competency focus
keyIdea.text: Explain architecture, identify threats, and inspect HTTP interactions to inform practical security testing.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes
screens.subtitle: What you can do after this chapter

narration.text: This second objectives screen focuses on actionable outcomes. You will be able to map a vulnerability to the stack layer it affects, for example recognizing when an injection flaw targets database queries versus when broken authentication is an app logic problem. You will also learn to evaluate the security of input validation: show that client-side checks are bypassable, and demonstrate why server-side validation is mandatory. You will practice capturing and interpreting a POST payload from a login form to verify how credentials are transmitted. Lastly, you will be able to explain to a developer whether a reported flaw is transport-related, server misconfiguration, or application logic, which helps prioritize fixes. A common misconception is equating transport encryption with secure applications. In practice, you must consider data handling and business logic even when HTTPS is present. These outcomes prepare you for the hands-on activity that follows, and they set expectations for responsible, permission-based testing.

keyIdea.title: Practical outcome
keyIdea.text: Translate observations from web traffic into precise, actionable findings for developers and defenders.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Practical Outcomes
Translate to Action

Convert traffic observations into clear remediation steps developers can implement.

Example outcome
Capture a login POST and show that missing server-side validation permits invalid input reaching the database.
Misconception
HTTPS prevents eavesdropping but does not stop SQL or logic errors on the server.
Inspect & Report

Learn the minimal evidence to collect: request/response headers, status codes, and example payloads that reproduce an issue.

Reporting tip
Show the exact request that demonstrates the flaw and explain why it violates server-side expectations.
Ethics
Only test systems when you have explicit written permission. Unauthorized testing is illegal and unethical.

screens.title: Client-Server Architecture
screens.subtitle: How browsers, web servers, application servers, and databases form a stack

narration.text: A web application is a layered system where each layer has a distinct responsibility and a distinct attack surface. The browser is the client that renders H T M L, C S S, and JavaScript and initiates HTTP requests. The web server receives those requests, serves static assets, and often forwards dynamic requests to an application server. The application server executes server-side code that enforces business logic, validates input, and interacts with a database for storage and retrieval. The database persists user data and can be a target for injection attacks if inputs are not handled correctly. As an example, consider a user loading a profile page: the browser issues a GET request; the web server routes it to the application server; the application server queries the database for the profile record and returns H T M L. A common misconception is that all logic runs in the browser — in reality, critical security checks and access control must happen on the server because client-side code can be modified or bypassed. When testing, map each observed behavior to the layer likely responsible. If you see an unexpected S Q L error in a response, the problem likely lies in how server-side code constructs database queries. If a page exposes administrative controls in the client without server checks, that is an authorization design flaw. Key takeaway: understanding these responsibilities helps you target tests where they are most effective.

keyIdea.title: Layered responsibilities
keyIdea.text: Each layer—client, web server, app server, database—has unique duties and unique vulnerabilities; match tests to layers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Client-Server Architecture
Architecture Overview
Understand responsibilities and failure points for each layer.
Browser (Client)
Renders content and runs scripts; cannot be trusted for security checks.
Web Server
Serves static files and routes dynamic requests to the app server; misconfigurations here expose endpoints.
App Server
Executes logic, validates input, enforces auth, and builds queries to the database.
Database
Stores data and must be protected from untrusted input to avoid injection.
Annotated Flow Example
Profile page request lifecycle (concrete scenario).
Step 1 — Browser GET /profile
Browser requests the profile page; query parameters may include user id.
Step 2 — Web Server Routes
Web server forwards dynamic requests to the app server or serves cached content.
Step 3 — App Server Query
Server-side code validates input, builds a query, and requests data from the database.
Step 4 — Database Response
Database returns data; server renders HTML and sends a response. If queries are constructed insecurely, injection is possible.
Key Takeaway

Map observed errors or behavior to the layer responsible — this directs where to test and how to explain the finding.

screens.title: HTTP and HTTPS
screens.subtitle: Stateless requests, methods, headers, and the role of TLS

narration.text: HTTP is the primary protocol browsers use to request resources from web servers. It is stateless, which means the server treats each request independently unless the application uses mechanisms like cookies or tokens to maintain state. HTTP methods such as GET and POST convey intent: GET typically retrieves data, while POST submits data that often includes user input. Headers carry metadata — user-agent, cookies, content type — that shape how the server processes a request. HTTPS wraps HTTP with TLS to encrypt the transport so eavesdroppers cannot read or tamper with requests. However, TLS does not validate the server’s logic or guarantee correct input handling on the server side. A practical example is inspecting a login form submission: over HTTP an attacker on the network could read credentials in transit; over HTTPS the credentials are encrypted, yet if the server stores passwords in plaintext or fails to validate input, the application is still vulnerable. A frequent misunderstanding is to assume that HTTPS eliminates all web vulnerabilities; in reality it primarily protects confidentiality and integrity in transit. When testing, confirm whether sensitive endpoints are served over HTTPS and then assess the application logic independently.

keyIdea.title: Protocol clarity
keyIdea.text: HTTP defines request/response exchange and methods; HTTPS secures transport but not application correctness.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › HTTP & HTTPS
Request Anatomy
GET /profile?id=42 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
User-Agent: ExampleBrowser/1.0
Accept: text/html
Cookie: session=abc123
This sample GET shows the request line, host, headers, and cookies. A POST will include a payload or form data in its body.
HTTPS vs HTTP
HTTPS encrypts traffic between client and server using TLS. It prevents passive interception and tampering but does not validate server-side code.
Example
A login form POST will encrypt credentials in transit under HTTPS, but if the server echoes input without sanitization it could still be vulnerable to cross-site scripting or injection when the server stores or renders that data.
Common mistake
Assuming HTTPS is a complete security solution. It secures transport only; application logic must still be correct and validated server-side.
Key Takeaway

Check both transport security and application behavior; secure transport does not imply secure application logic.

screens.title: State in a Stateless Protocol
screens.subtitle: How cookies, sessions, and tokens maintain user state across requests

narration.text: HTTP is stateless: each request is independent and the server does not remember previous requests by default. Web applications implement state through mechanisms such as cookies, server-side sessions, and tokens. A common pattern is that the server issues a Set-Cookie header after authentication, and the browser sends that cookie on subsequent requests to identify the user. Alternatively, the application may return a bearer token which the client stores and sends in an Authorization header. For example, when you log in, the server may create a server-side session record and return a cookie that contains a session identifier. The browser includes that cookie on later requests so the server can look up the session data and know who the user is. Attackers often target session handling: session fixation, session hijacking, or weak session identifiers can allow impersonation. A misconception is believing cookies are always secure by default. Cookie flags such as Secure and HttpOnly matter: without Secure, cookies can be exposed over unencrypted channels; without HttpOnly, scripts could read them. When testing, inspect Set-Cookie headers, session lifetimes, and whether sensitive actions require fresh validation. The key question is: does server-side logic correctly verify session ownership and permissions?

keyIdea.title: State management matters
keyIdea.text: Session and token handling determine user identity across requests; flaws enable impersonation or replay attacks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › State Management
Common Mechanisms
  • Cookies: Browser-stored key-value pairs set by Set-Cookie headers.
  • Server-side sessions: Server keeps session data indexed by a session id in a cookie.
  • Bearer tokens: Client stores token and sends it in Authorization headers for stateless APIs.
Example — Set-Cookie
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Secure; HttpOnly; Path=/; SameSite=Lax
Risks & Checks
Inspect cookie flags, session expiration, and whether sensitive operations require re-authentication.
Attack scenario
An attacker who steals a session id can impersonate a user if the server relies solely on that id without additional checks.
Pro Tip
Look for long-lived sessions, missing Secure/HttpOnly flags, and endpoints that accept only cookie-based auth without verifying origin or device.
Key Takeaway

Session handling is a primary target for attackers; verify flags, lifetime, and server-side ownership checks.

screens.title: Client-side vs Server-side Processing
screens.subtitle: Responsibilities, trust boundaries, and security implications

narration.text: Client-side code runs in the user's browser and is intended for presentation and immediate feedback, such as form formatting and simple validation. Server-side code runs in a controlled environment and must enforce all critical security checks, data validation, and access control. The key security difference is trust: client-side behavior cannot be trusted because an attacker can modify scripts, send crafted requests directly, or disable client checks. For example, a registration form may validate email format in JavaScript to improve user experience, but an attacker can bypass that validation and submit malformed or malicious input directly to the server. If server-side validation is missing, this can lead to injection or data corruption. Another common example is access control: hiding an administration button in the UI is insufficient if the server does not verify that the requesting user has admin privileges. A typical misconception is thinking client-side protections are security controls rather than UX features. When testing, always verify that the server enforces constraints and that sensitive operations require server-side authorization. The takeaway is simple: treat anything originating from the client as untrusted input and design server logic accordingly.

keyIdea.title: Trust boundary
keyIdea.text: Client-side = convenience; server-side = enforce security. Never trust client-originating data without server validation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Client vs Server
Client-side
Runs in the browser, used for UI, UX, and convenience checks.
Example
JavaScript validates an email pattern before the form is submitted to improve user experience.
Limitations
Any client-side check can be bypassed by modifying requests or disabling scripts.
Server-side
Runs on the server and must enforce validation, authentication, and authorization.
Example
Server verifies email format, checks for existing accounts, hashes passwords, and queries the database safely.
Best practice
Always treat client input as untrusted. Implement validation and authorization on the server.
Key Takeaway

Design server-side logic to expect manipulated client input; only use client checks for user experience.

screens.title: Injection Flaws (Overview)
screens.subtitle: When untrusted data becomes code or a query

narration.text: Injection occurs when an application sends untrusted data to an interpreter as part of a command or query. The most familiar example is S Q L injection, where user input is embedded into a database query and the interpreter executes unintended commands. Injection is powerful because it allows an attacker to change the intended semantics of a query. A concrete scenario: a search field constructs an S Q L query by concatenating user input directly into the statement. If the input contains injection payloads, the database may return data beyond the user's scope or even allow data modification. Injection is not limited to S Q L; it can target other interpreters such as OS commands, LDAP, or NoSQL queries. A common misconception is believing only complex payloads succeed; simple misplaced quotes or missing parameterization are often sufficient. Defenses include prepared statements, parameterized queries, and strict input handling on the server. When testing, look for fields that interact with backend storage or system commands and try to determine whether input is concatenated into queries. The key question to ask is whether the server uses safe parameter binding or builds queries directly from raw input.

keyIdea.title: Injection risk
keyIdea.text: Untrusted input that reaches an interpreter without parameterization can change program behavior; parameterized queries are a primary defense.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Injection Flaws
What is Injection?

When user-controlled data is interpreted as code or part of a query, allowing an attacker to change the intended command.

Example — vulnerable query
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + input + "'"
Defense
Use parameterized queries or prepared statements so input is treated as data, not code.
Testing & Misconceptions
Not all injection payloads are complex; often unescaped quotes or special characters reveal vulnerabilities.
Where to test
Fields that interact with databases, system commands, or interpreters. Try boundary characters and parameterized attempts.
Common mistake
Assuming length checks or client-side validation prevent injection — they do not if server concatenates input into queries.
Key Takeaway

If input reaches an interpreter, ensure it is passed safely as data. Parameterize queries to prevent injection.

screens.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
screens.subtitle: Injecting client-side scripts into pages viewed by other users

narration.text: Cross-site scripting allows an attacker to inject malicious client-side scripts into pages that other users view. XSS often occurs when server-side code reflects or stores user input and then renders it into a page without proper escaping or encoding. There are common forms: reflected XSS where a payload is returned immediately in a response, and stored XSS where the payload is saved in a database and served to other users later. A concrete example is a comment field that accepts H T M L and stores it in the database; when other users view the comment, the malicious script executes in their browsers, potentially stealing cookies or manipulating the DOM. Defenses include context-sensitive output encoding, Content Security Policy, and sanitization of untrusted H T M L inputs. A frequent misconception is that input validation alone solves XSS; while validation helps, proper output encoding for the specific H T M L context is critical because safe characters depend on whether input is placed inside an attribute, H T M L body, or JavaScript context. When testing, try harmless script payloads to see if content is rendered as code and observe whether sensitive cookies are accessible. The key question: does the server render untrusted input into a user’s page without appropriate encoding?

keyIdea.title: XSS risk
keyIdea.text: XSS lets attackers run scripts in victims' browsers: fix it by encoding output for the rendering context and minimizing unsafe HTML acceptance.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Cross-Site Scripting
XSS Explained

An attacker injects client-side code that executes in other users' browsers when rendered without proper encoding.

Example — stored XSS
<script>fetch('/steal?cookie='+document.cookie)</script>
Defense
Apply context-aware encoding and consider Content Security Policy and sanitization of allowed HTML inputs.
Testing & Misconceptions
Not every script payload will run depending on context; test for reflection, storage, and execution contexts separately.
Where to probe
Any user input that is later displayed: comments, profile fields, search results, and error messages.
Common mistake
Assuming HTML stripping alone is sufficient. Correct encoding for the specific output context is required.
Key Takeaway

Treat any rendered user input as untrusted; encode for the output context and avoid unsafe HTML acceptance where possible.

narration.text: Broken authentication and session management refer to weaknesses that let attackers bypass authentication, hijack sessions, or reuse credentials beyond their intended scope. Common problems include weak or predictable session identifiers, missing expiration or rotation, improper logout handling, and failure to validate credentials on sensitive actions. For a concrete example, imagine an application that issues session ids with low entropy and accepts them indefinitely. An attacker who can guess or brute-force a session id may impersonate a legitimate user. Another scenario is when an application does not revalidate the user's identity for critical actions such as changing an email address; an attacker with an active session could perform the change. Defenses include strong, random session tokens, short lifetimes, secure cookie flags, and reauthentication for high-risk transactions. A frequent misconception is that successful login throttling is the only defense; in reality, session handling and token lifecycle matter equally. When testing, look for predictable session ids, long-lived sessions, and endpoints that perform sensitive changes without verifying the current credential or requiring a second factor. The closing question: could an attacker use an existing session or weak token to act as another user?

keyIdea.title: Authentication fragility
keyIdea.text: Weak tokens, long sessions, and missing reauthentication expose users to impersonation; protect tokens and require strong session controls.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Broken Authentication
What can go wrong
  • Predictable or guessable session or token values.
  • Missing Secure/HttpOnly flags on cookies.
  • Sessions that do not expire or are not invalidated on logout.
Example
An attacker obtains a session id and uses it to access user data if the server does not verify more than the id.
Checks & Remedies
Verify token randomness, enforce short lifetimes, use secure cookie flags, and require reauthentication for sensitive changes.
Pro Test
Attempt session fixation by setting a known session id before login and observe whether the server accepts it post-login.
Common mistake
Assuming HTTPS alone prevents token theft. Client-side XSS can steal tokens unless HttpOnly is set.
Key Takeaway

Treat session tokens as high-value secrets: protect their creation, storage, and lifecycle, and require reauthentication for sensitive operations.

screens.title: Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR)
screens.subtitle: When parameter manipulation exposes unauthorized resources

narration.text: Insecure Direct Object References occur when an application exposes internal object references such as database keys, file names, or identifiers, and does not enforce authorization checks. An attacker can manipulate these references to access resources belonging to other users. For instance, if a profile endpoint accepts a numeric id like /profile? id=100 and the server only uses that id to fetch and return data without verifying the requesting user's rights, an attacker who changes the id to 101 could view someone else's profile. IDORs are often the result of failing to combine authentication information with the requested resource when enforcing access control. A common misconception is trusting obscurity: changing identifiers to non-sequential values reduces casual guessing but does not replace authorization checks. Defenses include enforcing access control on the server using the authenticated user's identity, avoiding direct exposure of internal identifiers where possible, and mapping references to access checks. When testing, try adjusting resource identifiers and observe whether the application enforces ownership or returns unauthorized data. The question to ask: does the server verify that the authenticated user is allowed to access the requested object?

keyIdea.title: Authorization check
keyIdea.text: Always validate that the authenticated user is permitted to access a referenced object; opaque identifiers alone are not sufficient.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › IDOR
IDOR Example
An endpoint returns an object when given an id, but fails to verify ownership.
Scenario
GET /document?doc_id=123 returns document 123 for the requesting user without checking whether that user owns document 123.
Test
Modify the identifier to other values and observe whether the server blocks access or returns other users' data.
Mitigations
Check ownership server-side, map references to user context, and avoid exposing internal keys directly when possible.
Developer fix
When handling a request for an object, validate that the authenticated user has the rights to access that object before returning it.
Common mistake
Believing that non-sequential or hashed IDs prevent abuse. Without authorization checks these measures only slow attackers, not stop them.
Key Takeaway

Always enforce server-side authorization for every object access, tying resource retrieval to the authenticated user.

screens.title: Inspecting HTTP Traffic with Browser DevTools
screens.subtitle: Capture requests, headers, and payloads using a browser network panel

narration.text: The browser's developer tools let you observe the exact HTTP requests and responses between the browser and server. In this activity you will practice capturing a GET request for a page and a POST request for a login form. Start by opening developer tools and selecting the Network tab. Refresh the page to see all requests that load the page. Click a request entry to view its headers and status code: you will see the Request URL, Method, Status, Request Headers, and Response Headers. For a POST request, examine the Payload or Form Data sub-tab to see how the username and password were sent. If you see a Set-Cookie header in the response, note whether the cookie has Secure and HttpOnly flags. A practical example is submitting dummy credentials to a test login page and observing the POST body and resulting Set-Cookie header. A common misconception is that developer tools change request behavior; they only show what the browser sends and receives. When testing, clear previous requests for a focused view, reproduce the action, and capture a single request showing the full header and payload set. Always perform this activity on a site you control or have permission to test. The final check: can you identify the authentication cookie and the exact parameter names used in the request?

keyIdea.title: Observation skill
keyIdea.text: Use Network tools to capture request/response details, inspect payloads, and verify cookie flags to support findings.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › DevTools — Network
Step-by-step
  1. Open browser developer tools and select the Network tab.
  2. Refresh the page to capture requests; click the main document request to inspect headers and status.
  3. Submit a login form and inspect the new POST request's Payload or Form Data.
  4. Check response headers for Set-Cookie and note flags like Secure and HttpOnly.
Example Payload
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=test&password=test
What to observe
  • Request Method and URL to identify the endpoint.
  • Request and Response Headers for authentication and cookies.
  • Response status codes and payloads to detect errors or leakage.
Ethical note
Perform these actions only on sites you control or have explicit permission to test.
Key Takeaway

A captured request with headers and payload is reliable evidence for reporting and helps pinpoint where defenses are missing.

screens.title: Web Servers vs Application Servers
screens.subtitle: Roles, examples, and where vulnerabilities often appear

narration.text: Web servers and application servers are distinct components that together deliver web applications. A web server such as Nginx, Apache, or IIS primarily serves static content like images, C S S, and H T M L, and it can act as a reverse proxy or load balancer. It routes dynamic requests to an application server. Application servers — Node. js, Tomcat, Gunicorn — execute dynamic code, implement business logic, and interact with databases. Vulnerabilities can appear at both layers: misconfigured web servers can expose directory listings, default files, or management interfaces; application servers may expose debug endpoints or have insecure default settings. A concrete example is a web server misconfiguration that allows access to a backup file containing credentials. Another is an application server exposing a debug console in production. When testing, check server headers, exposed directories, and default pages on the web server, and review the application server for unprotected management endpoints and verbose error messages that leak implementation details. A common misconception is that only application code can cause logic flaws; in reality, a web server misconfiguration can produce critical exposures. The central question is: which layer controls the behavior you're observing, and what defensive configuration should be corrected?

keyIdea.title: Different layers, different fixes
keyIdea.text: Web server misconfigurations and application server logic issues both create risks; identify the responsible layer to recommend the correct remediation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Web vs App Server
Web Server
Serves static assets, manages TLS, and routes requests. Check for exposed directories and default pages.
Common issues
Directory listing enabled, misconfigured proxy, or outdated server banners that reveal versions.
Application Server
Executes dynamic code, enforces business rules, and queries databases. Look for debug endpoints and verbose errors.
Common issues
Exposed admin consoles, unsafe default configs, and unhandled exceptions that leak stack traces.
Key Takeaway

Identify whether an issue stems from server configuration or application logic to prescribe an accurate fix.

Pro Tip
Examine response headers, default pages, and any exposed management endpoints to determine the responsible layer.

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential points you should retain. First, web applications are layered: browsers, web servers, application servers, and databases each play different roles and can fail in different ways. Second, HTTP is stateless; cookies, sessions, and tokens provide state, and session handling must be robust to avoid impersonation. Third, HTTPS secures transport but does not fix application logic; always evaluate server-side behavior independently. Fourth, common threats include injection, XSS, broken authentication, and IDOR; each maps to a different part of the stack. Fifth, client-side validation improves UX but cannot be relied on for security. Finally, browser developer tools are invaluable for observing requests, headers, and payloads to gather evidence. As you move forward, use these concepts to choose focused tests, explain findings clearly, and recommend precise remediations. Key Concepts means layered architecture and precise observation guide both testing and remediation; transport security and application security are distinct responsibilities.. In practical terms, what to remember. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

HTTP / HTTPS
Transport protocol; HTTPS encrypts transit but not server logic.
Server & DB
Web servers route; app servers run logic; databases store data and are injection targets.
State & Sessions
Cookies, tokens, and server sessions maintain state; protect their lifecycle and flags.
Summary Takeaway
Use layered understanding and network observations to find and explain vulnerabilities accurately.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact cards to keep handy

narration.text: Keep these three quick reminders in mind as you test: First, always treat client input as untrusted; perform validation and authorization on the server. Second, HTTPS protects transport confidentiality and integrity but does not replace secure coding or server checks. Third, use browser developer tools to capture requests, headers, and payloads as reproducible evidence. These reminders will help you decide what to test, how to collect meaningful evidence, and how to communicate a finding to developers in a way that leads to a fix. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Trust nothing from client
Always validate and authorize on the server.
HTTPS protects transport
But you must still fix server-side logic and configuration.
Capture reproducible evidence
Use dev tools to show requests, headers, and payloads when reporting issues.
Final thought
Combine layered understanding with measured observation to find meaningful, fixable vulnerabilities.
